entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms, lasting a few seconds, that moves oddly and may vanish with a bang. No accepted explanation exists, and few photographs or recordings of it exist.
entries.background: Reported for centuries, mostly by chance eyewitnesses. Scientists have proposed many theories but none is widely accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist who wrote about thunder and lightning in 1837. His writing gave 'ball lightning' its name in science.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: German school official who wrote 'Der Kugelblitz' (1923), a collection of ball lightning cases and the only German-language book on the subject.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who keeps a database of Russian ball lightning reports and has co-written a book on the subject.

entries.name: Stenhoff
entries.background: Author of a 1999 book on ball lightning that cites about 2400 references and collects many witness reports.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: Turner's description of ball lightning research as split between people who collect reports, theorists and lab experimenters, with little coordination.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A US network of cameras that photographed the night sky to track meteors. Researchers searched its photographs and found two probable ball lightning events.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's network of sensors that records the time, place and strength of lightning strikes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: Germany's lightning location service, which records where and when strokes hit and how strong they are.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist and a member of the Vienna academy of sciences. He saw and sketched a ball in a thunderstorm in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen University observatory who, as a child in 1951, saw a ball split into smaller balls that melted patches of asphalt.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale, famous for dinosaur fossil discoveries, who also led the US National Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist known for the 1922 Stern–Gerlach experiment, which showed that atoms' magnetic orientation comes in discrete values.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer who, as a passenger on a 1963 night flight, saw a glowing ball drift down the aisle. His report in Nature drew wide media attention.

entries.name: Alfred Brian Pippard
entries.background: British physicist, professor at Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory and Fellow of the Royal Society, known for work on metals at low temperatures.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist in St Petersburg who was killed by lightning in 1753 while experimenting on atmospheric electricity.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician in Paris who founded modern neurology and taught Sigmund Freud. He studied nerve disorders at the Salpêtrière Hospital.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: Short-lived paralysis and nerve effects caused by lightning, set apart from the longer-lasting trauma-related nervous disorder that can follow.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.senseHere: A 1936 report from Dorstone, England, of a red-hot ball that fell into a tub of water and made it boil. It is used to estimate the energy such a ball can hold.

entries.name: Poughquag glass
entries.senseHere: A 2008 sighting at a home in Poughquag, New York, where the glass of the porch door was later measured for glow caused by radiation from the ball.

entries.name: Camp Blanding
entries.background: A military base in Florida where researchers fire rockets trailing wires to trigger lightning for experiments.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.senseHere: A 2012 recording in China of a ball lightning event by two video cameras fitted with light-splitting gratings. It showed the ball's light contained iron, calcium, silicon, nitrogen and oxygen.
